note: Math trainer problem types. Vars are generated per level, steps are evaluated in order with Godot Expression and the helpers in src/math/math_functions.gd. NEC values come from data/nec/<edition>/tables.json through t()/trange()/v(); non-NEC constants through k().

labels.squirrel_cage: three-phase squirrel-cage motor (not Design B energy-efficient)

types.title: Find current (I = E ÷ R)
types.prompt: A heater element with a resistance of {R} Ω is connected to {E} volts. How much current does it draw?
types.hint: Cover I on the Ohm's law wheel: E is over R, so divide.

steps.note: Current (I, amps) equals voltage (E, volts) divided by resistance (R, ohms).
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Find voltage (E = I × R)
types.prompt: A current of {I} A flows through a {R} Ω resistor. What is the voltage across the resistor?
types.hint: Cover E on the Ohm's law wheel: I and R sit side by side, so multiply.

steps.note: Voltage (E) equals current (I) times resistance (R).

types.title: Find resistance (R = E ÷ I)
types.prompt: A load on a {E} V circuit draws {I} A. What is the resistance of the load?
types.hint: Cover R on the Ohm's law wheel: E is over I, so divide.

steps.note: Resistance (R, ohms) equals voltage (E) divided by current (I).
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Current from watts (I = P ÷ E)
types.prompt: A {P} W load is connected to {E} volts. What current does it draw?
types.hint: Cover I on the power wheel: P is over E, so divide watts by volts.

steps.note: Current (amps) equals power (watts) divided by voltage (volts).
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Watts (P = E × I)
types.prompt: A motor on a {E} V circuit draws {I} A. How many watts does it use (assume a power factor of 1)?
types.hint: Cover P on the power wheel: I and E sit side by side, so multiply.

steps.note: Power (watts) equals voltage times current.

types.title: Watts from current (P = I² × R)
types.prompt: A {I} A current flows through a {R} Ω conductor. How many watts are lost as heat?
types.hint: Square the current first (I × I), then multiply by R.

steps.note: Power (watts) equals current squared times resistance. I² means I × I.

types.title: Three-phase current (I = P ÷ (E × 1.732))
types.prompt: A balanced three-phase load of {kw} kW (power factor 1) is supplied at {E} volts. What is the line current?
types.hint: Three-phase: multiply the volts by 1.732 first, then divide the watts by that number.

steps.note: Three-phase current equals watts divided by (line volts × √3). √3 is about 1.732.
Store this in memory (M+) so you can divide by it next.
On a scientific calculator you can type it all at once: {P} ÷ ( {E} × {s3} ) =

types.title: Series resistance
types.prompt: Resistors of {list} are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
types.hint: In series, just add every resistor together.

vars.expr: join_nonzero([R1, R2, R3, R4], ' Ω, ') + ' Ω'

steps.note: In a series circuit the current has one path, so the resistances add up.

types.title: Equal resistors in parallel (Rt = R ÷ n)
types.prompt: A circuit contains {n} resistors of {R} Ω each, connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
types.hint: Equal resistors in parallel: divide one resistor's value by how many there are.

steps.note: Identical resistors in parallel: one resistor's value divided by the number of resistors. The total is always smaller than any one resistor.
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Two resistors in parallel (product over sum)
types.prompt: A {R1} Ω resistor and a {R2} Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
types.hint: Multiply the two values, then divide by their sum (product over sum).

steps.note: Product over sum works for exactly two resistors in parallel.
Scientific calculator in one go: ( {R1} × {R2} ) ÷ ( {R1} + {R2} ) =
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Three resistors in parallel (reciprocal method)
types.prompt: Resistors of {R1} Ω, {R2} Ω and {R3} Ω are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
types.hint: Take 1 ÷ each resistor, add those up, then take 1 ÷ the total.

steps.note: Works for any number of resistors in parallel.
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Resistance vs. length and size
types.prompt: A conductor has a resistance of {R1} Ω. What is the resistance of a conductor of the same material that is {lf} times as long and has {af} of the cross-sectional area?
types.hint: Longer wire means more resistance (multiply). Smaller wire means more resistance too (divide by the area fraction).

steps.note: Resistance goes up with length and down with cross-sectional area.

steps.text: Area is 1/{ad}, so resistance is {ad} times: × {ad} = {Rl} Ω

types.title: Box fill: required volume
types.prompt: A box will contain {n} {awg:awg} insulated conductors{extras}. What minimum box volume is required by 314.16(B)?
types.hint: Count allowances: each conductor 1, all clamps together 1, each device yoke 2, up to four EGCs together 1. Then multiply by the Table 314.16(B)(1) volume.

vars.expr: pick(clamps + yokes + egc == 0, '', ' plus ' + join_nonempty([pick(clamps > 0, 'internal cable clamps', ''), pick(yokes > 0, plural(yokes, 'device yoke', 'device yokes'), ''), pick(egc > 0, plural(egc, 'equipment grounding conductor', 'equipment grounding conductors'), '')], ', '))

steps.note: 314.16(B): count allowances, then use Table 314.16(B)(1) for the volume of one conductor of that size.
314.16(B)(1): each conductor that starts or ends in the box counts 1.
314.16(B)(2): one allowance for all internal cable clamps together.
314.16(B)(4): each yoke (switch or receptacle) counts 2.
314.16(B)(5): one allowance for up to four EGCs together.

steps.text: EGCs: 1 for the first four + ¼ × {egc_x} extra = + {xe1} (total {cnt})
steps.note: 314.16(B)(5): one allowance for up to four EGCs, plus ¼ allowance for each one over four.

types.title: Box fill: how many conductors fit
types.prompt: How many {awg:awg} conductors may be installed in a {box} box{extras_q}?
types.hint: Take the box volume from Table 314.16(A), divide by the conductor volume from Table 314.16(B)(1), and drop any fraction. Subtract other allowances first.

vars.expr: pick(clamps + yokes == 0, '', ' that also has ' + join_nonempty([pick(clamps > 0, 'internal cable clamps', ''), pick(yokes > 0, plural(yokes, 'device yoke', 'device yokes'), '')], ' and '))

steps.text: Conductors = box volume ÷ volume per conductor
steps.note: Always round down: a part of a conductor does not fit.
Each yoke takes 2 allowances; all clamps together take 1.

types.title: Conduit fill: how many wires fit
types.prompt: How many {awg:awg} {ins_name} conductors may be installed in trade size {ts} {rw_name}{nip_text}?
types.hint: Take the 40% area for the raceway (Chapter 9, Table 4; 60% for a nipple of 24 in. or less), divide by one wire's area (Table 5). Round up only if the decimal is 0.8 or more (Note 7).

steps.text: Wires = {pct_text} raceway area ÷ one wire's area
steps.note: {fill_rule}
show: pick(nipple == 1, 'Chapter 9, Note 4: a nipple 24 in. or shorter may be filled to 60%.', 'Chapter 9, Table 1: over 2 wires may fill 40% of the raceway.')

steps.text: Chapter 9, Table 4, {rw_name} trade size {ts}, {pct_text} column = {A} in²

show: pick(frac(q) >= v('ch9.note7_round_up_at') - 0.0000001, 'The decimal is 0.8 or more, so round up (Note 7):', 'The decimal is under 0.8, so drop it (Note 7):')
steps.note: Chapter 9, Note 7: round up only when the decimal is 0.8 or larger.

types.title: Conduit fill: pick the raceway size
types.prompt: What minimum trade size {rw_name} is required for {n} {awg:awg} {ins_name} conductors?
types.hint: Multiply one wire's area (Table 5) by the number of wires, then find the first raceway whose 40% column is at least that big (Table 4).

steps.note: Chapter 9, Table 1: over 2 wires may fill 40% of the raceway.

steps.text: Chapter 9, Table 4, {rw_name}: trade size {ts} holds {A} in² at 40%, the first size that is at least {tot} in²

types.title: Ampacity with correction and adjustment
types.prompt: What is the ampacity of a {size:awg} {metal_name} {ins} conductor in an ambient temperature of {ambient}°F with {ccc} current-carrying conductors in the raceway?
types.hint: Start with Table 310.16, multiply by the temperature correction factor, then by the adjustment factor for more than three current-carrying conductors.

steps.note: 310.15(B) corrects for hot or cold rooms. 310.15(C)(1) adjusts for more than three current-carrying conductors.

steps.text: Table 310.15(B)(1)(1): {ambient}°F is in the {amb_row} °F row, {temp}°C column = {corr}
Table 310.15(C)(1): {ccc} conductors is in the {ccc_row} row = {adj_pct}% = {adj}
3 or fewer current-carrying conductors: no adjustment (× 1.00)

steps.note: Keep up to three decimal places.

types.title: Voltage drop, single-phase (2KIL ÷ CM)
types.prompt: A {E} V single-phase load draws {I} A at a distance of {L} ft (one way) using {size:awg} {metal_name} conductors. What is the voltage drop?
types.hint: VD = 2 × K × I × L ÷ CM. L is the one-way distance; the 2 counts the trip out and back. CM comes from Chapter 9, Table 8.

steps.note: K = resistance constant, I = amps, L = one-way length in feet, CM = circular mils of the wire.
K is a textbook constant (ohms per circular-mil-foot), not an NEC table value.
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Voltage drop, three-phase (1.732KIL ÷ CM)
types.prompt: A {E} V three-phase load draws {I} A at a distance of {L} ft using {size:awg} {metal_name} conductors. What is the voltage drop?
types.hint: Three-phase uses 1.732 instead of 2: VD = 1.732 × K × I × L ÷ CM.

steps.note: Three-phase circuits use √3 (1.732) in place of 2.
K is a textbook constant (ohms per circular-mil-foot), not an NEC table value.
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Percent voltage drop
types.prompt: You have {Vs} volts at the panel and {Vl} volts at the load. What is the percentage of voltage drop?
types.hint: Subtract to get the drop, divide by the panel (source) voltage, then × 100.

steps.text: % drop = (V source − V load) ÷ V source × 100
steps.note: Always divide by the source (panel) voltage.
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Dwelling general lighting demand
types.prompt: {intro} What is the demand load for general lighting, small-appliance and laundry circuits (standard method)?
types.hint: Area × 3 VA, plus 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit. Then Table 220.45: first 3,000 VA at 100%, next up to 120,000 VA at 35%, the rest at 25%.

vars.expr: pick(units == 1, 'A ' + fmt(area) + ' ft² dwelling has ' + fmt(sa) + ' small-appliance circuits and one laundry circuit.', 'An apartment building has ' + fmt(units) + ' units. Each unit is ' + fmt(area) + ' ft² with 2 small-appliance circuits and one laundry circuit.')

steps.text: Lighting + small appliance + laundry, then demand factors
steps.note: 220.41 (3 VA per ft²), 220.52(A) and (B) (1,500 VA per circuit), Table 220.45 demand factors.
220.52(A): at least two 20-ampere small-appliance circuits (210.11(C)(1)).
3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%: the whole 117,000 VA band.
Add the pieces together.

types.title: Dwelling service load (standard method)
types.prompt: A {area} ft² dwelling has 2 small-appliance circuits, a laundry circuit, a {rkw} kW range, a {dry} W dryer, a {wh} W water heater, a {dw} W dishwasher, a {disp} W disposal{extra_text}, {heat} kW of electric heat and a {ac} VA air conditioner. What is the minimum service load in amperes at 120/240 V (standard method)?
types.hint: Work down the list: lighting demand, range (Table 220.55), dryer (220.54, at least 5,000 W), fixed appliances (75% if four or more), the larger of heat or A/C, then divide by 240 V.

vars.expr: pick(extra > 0, ', a ' + fmt(extra) + ' W built-in microwave', '')

steps.text: Service = lighting + range + dryer + appliances + larger of heat or A/C
steps.note: Standard method, Article 220 Parts II and III. Divide the total VA by 240 V.

steps.text: Range: Table 220.55, Column C, 1 range = {r_base} kW{r_note} → {r_va} VA
show: pick(r_over > 0, ', + ' + fmt(r_over * 5) + '% (Note 1: ' + fmt(r_over) + ' kW over 12) = ' + fmt(r(r_base * (1 + r_over * 0.05), 3)) + ' kW', '')

steps.text: Dryer: larger of {dry} W or 5,000 W = {dry_va} VA
steps.note: 220.54: at least 5,000 W or the nameplate, whichever is larger.
Water heater, dishwasher, disposal and similar appliances fastened in place.
220.53: 75% demand for four or more fastened-in-place appliances.
220.53 applies only to four or more appliances.

steps.text: Heat {heat_va} VA vs. A/C {ac} VA: use the larger = {hvac} VA
steps.note: 220.60: noncoincident loads, use only the larger.

types.title: Range demand (Table 220.55)
types.prompt: {intro} What is the demand load in kW?
types.hint: Column C gives the demand for ranges up to 12 kW. For bigger ranges, add 5% to the Column C value for each kW (or major fraction) over 12 kW (Note 1).

vars.expr: pick(n == 1, 'A ' + fmt(kw) + ' kW range is installed in a dwelling unit.', fmt(n) + ' ranges rated ' + fmt(kw) + ' kW each are installed in an apartment building.')

steps.note: Table 220.55, Column C and Note 1.

show: trange_text('t220_55', n, 'col_c_expr').get_slice(' + ', 1).replace('n', name('', n)).replace('*', '×') + ' + ' + trange_text('t220_55', n, 'col_c_expr').get_slice(' + ', 0) + ' ='
steps.note: For 26 or more ranges Column C is a formula: n = {n} ranges.

steps.text: {kw} kW is not over 12 kW, so Column C applies as is: {dem} kW

steps.note: Note 1: each kW or major fraction (more than half) of a kW counts.

types.title: Dryer demand (Table 220.54)
types.prompt: {n} electric clothes dryers rated {w} W each are installed in a multifamily building. What is the demand load in kW?
types.hint: Each dryer counts at least 5,000 W (or its nameplate if bigger). Add them up, then use the Table 220.54 percentage for the number of dryers.

steps.note: 220.54: use 5,000 W or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger.

steps.text: Each dryer: larger of {w} W or 5,000 W = {each} W

types.title: Dryer feeder neutral (220.61(B))
types.prompt: What is the feeder neutral demand for {n} household electric clothes dryers rated {w} W each?
types.hint: Work out the Table 220.54 dryer demand first, then take 70% of it for the neutral (220.61(B)(1)).

steps.note: 220.61(B)(1): a 70% demand factor is permitted on the neutral for household dryers figured with Table 220.54.

steps.text: Each dryer: larger of {w} W or 5,000 W = {each} W

types.title: Cooking appliances, Column B (Table 220.55 Note 3)
types.prompt: What is the demand load for {n} household cooking appliances rated {kw} kW each (use Column B, Note 3)?
types.hint: Add the nameplate ratings, then multiply by the Column B percentage for the number of appliances. Column B is for appliances from 3½ kW through 8¾ kW.

steps.text: Demand = total nameplate kW × Column B %
steps.note: Table 220.55, Note 3: permitted instead of Column C for appliances over 1¾ kW through 8¾ kW.

types.title: Motor full-load current (Tables 430.248/250)
types.prompt: What full-load current is used to size the conductors for a {hp} hp, {V} V, {phase_name} induction motor?
types.hint: 430.6(A)(1): use the table current, not the nameplate. Single-phase is Table 430.248, three-phase is Table 430.250.

steps.text: Use the table current, not the nameplate
steps.note: 430.6(A)(1): conductor and overcurrent sizing use the NEC table full-load current.

types.title: Motor branch-circuit conductor (125%)
types.prompt: What minimum conductor ampacity is required for a {hp} hp, {V} V, {phase_name} motor (single motor, continuous duty)?
types.hint: Find the table full-load current (Table 430.248 single-phase, 430.250 three-phase) and multiply by 125% (430.22).

steps.note: 430.22: a single continuous-duty motor needs conductors rated at least 125% of its full-load current.

types.title: Motor overload protection (430.32)
types.prompt: A motor has a nameplate full-load current of {fla} A and {marking}. What is the maximum rating of the separate overload device?
types.hint: Overloads use the nameplate current. 125% if the service factor is 1.15 or more or the temperature rise is 40°C or less; 115% for all other motors.

vars.expr: pick(mk == 1, 'a service factor of 1.15', pick(mk == 2, 'a marked temperature rise of 40°C', 'a service factor of 1.0'))

steps.text: Overloads are sized from the nameplate
steps.note: 430.6(A)(2): separate motor overload protection is based on the motor nameplate current.

show: pick(mk == 1, 'service factor 1.15 or more', pick(mk == 2, 'temperature rise 40°C or less', 'all other motors'))

types.title: Motor short-circuit/ground-fault protection (430.52)
types.prompt: What is the maximum {device_name} rating for the branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection of a {hp} hp, {V} V, {motor_name}?
types.hint: Table FLC × the Table 430.52(C)(1) percentage for the device type. If that is not a standard size, 430.52(C)(1)(a) lets you go up to the next standard size in 240.6(A).

vars.expr: pick(dev == 'inverse_breaker', 'inverse time circuit breaker', pick(dev == 'dual_fuse', 'dual-element (time-delay) fuse', 'nontime-delay fuse'))

steps.note: Then 430.52(C)(1)(a) permits the next higher standard size.

steps.text: Next standard size (240.6(A)) at or above {raw} A = {ocpd} A
steps.note: 430.52(C)(1)(a): where the value is not a standard size, the next higher standard size is permitted.

types.title: Single-phase transformer current
types.prompt: What is the full-load secondary current of a {kva} kVA single-phase transformer with a {E} V secondary?
types.hint: Change kVA to VA (× 1,000), then divide by the voltage.

steps.note: Single-phase: volt-amperes divided by volts.
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Three-phase transformer current
types.prompt: What is the full-load {side} current of a {kva} kVA three-phase transformer at {E} V?
types.hint: Three-phase: I = VA ÷ (E × 1.732). Multiply E × 1.732 first.

steps.note: Three-phase: volt-amperes divided by (line volts × √3).
Scientific calculator in one go: {VA} ÷ ( {E} × {s3} ) =
Round to two decimal places.

types.title: Percent of a number
types.prompt: What is {p}% of {x}?
types.hint: Change the percent to a decimal (move the point two places left), then multiply.

steps.note: Percent means per hundred: 80% = 0.80, 125% = 1.25.

types.title: Efficiency (output ÷ input)
types.prompt: A motor delivers {hp} hp of output while drawing {win} W of input power. What is its efficiency?
types.hint: Change horsepower to watts (× 746), then efficiency = output ÷ input × 100.

steps.note: Both must be in the same units (watts).
Round to one decimal place.

types.title: Percent to fraction
types.prompt: {p}% is equivalent to what fraction?
types.hint: Write it over 100, then divide top and bottom by the biggest number that goes into both.

steps.note: Percent means per hundred.

steps.text: The biggest number that divides both {num0} and {den0} is {g}

steps.note: Check on the calculator: {p} ÷ 100 and {fn} ÷ {fd} give the same decimal.

types.title: Time for part of an AC cycle
types.prompt: A {hz} Hz sine wave travels {deg} degrees in how many seconds?
types.hint: One full cycle is 360° and takes 1/Hz seconds. Find what fraction of 360° you have.

steps.note: One cycle = 360°. At 60 Hz one cycle takes 1/60 of a second.
Compare the decimal with each choice: 1 ÷ 240 = 0.00417.

types.title: Scale drawings
types.prompt: A plan is drawn at a scale of {scale_text} inch = 1 foot. A dimension of {inch} inches on the drawing equals how many feet?
types.hint: Divide the drawing inches by the inches that stand for one foot.

steps.note: At 1/4 in = 1 ft, every 1/4 inch is one foot, so there are 4 feet per inch.

types.title: Commercial lighting load (Table 220.42(A))
types.prompt: Disregarding demand factors, what is the calculated general lighting load for a {area} ft² {occ_label}?
types.hint: Find the VA per square foot for the occupancy in Table 220.42(A) and multiply by the area.

steps.note: Table 220.42(A) gives the unit load per square foot for each occupancy.

types.title: Multioutlet assembly load (220.14(H))
types.prompt: What is the calculated load of a {L} ft fixed multioutlet assembly where the appliances are not likely to be used at the same time?
types.hint: 220.14(H)(1): 180 VA for each 5 ft or fraction of 5 ft. Round the number of sections up.

steps.note: 220.14(H)(1): each 5 ft or fraction of 5 ft counts as one outlet of 180 VA.

steps.text: Any fraction counts, so round up: {sec} sections

types.title: Busbar ampacity from area (366.23(A))
types.prompt: What is the maximum continuous current for a {area} in² {metal_name} busbar in an auxiliary gutter?
types.hint: 366.23(A): copper bars 1,000 A per square inch, aluminum 700 A per square inch.

steps.note: 366.23(A): 1,000 A per in² for copper, 700 A per in² for aluminum.

types.title: Busbar ampacity from size (366.23(A))
types.prompt: A {metal_name} busbar is {wd} in. wide by {th} in. thick. What is its maximum continuous current (366.23(A))?
types.hint: Width × thickness gives the area in square inches. Then × 1,000 for copper (700 for aluminum).

steps.text: Amps = width × thickness × amps per in²
steps.note: 366.23(A): 1,000 A per in² for copper, 700 A per in² for aluminum.

types.title: Arc welder overcurrent device (630.12(A))
types.prompt: An arc welder has an I1max rating of {i1} A. What is the maximum rating of the overcurrent device supplying it?
types.hint: 630.12(A): not more than 200% of I1max. If that is not a standard size, the next higher standard rating (240.6(A)) is permitted.

steps.text: Next standard rating (240.6(A)) at or above {raw} A = {ocpd} A
steps.note: 630.12(A) permits the next higher standard rating when 200% is not a standard size.

types.title: Resistance welder conductors (630.31(A))
types.prompt: What is the minimum ampacity of the supply conductors for a resistance welder with a duty cycle of {duty}% and a primary current of {ip} A?
types.hint: Multiply the primary current by the Table 630.31(A) multiplier for the duty cycle.

steps.note: 630.31(A)(2): for a resistance welder with a known duty cycle, use Table 630.31(A).

types.title: 10-foot feeder tap (240.21(B)(1))
types.prompt: For a field-installed feeder tap not over 10 ft long, what is the maximum rating of the feeder overcurrent device if the tap conductors have an ampacity of {tap} A?
types.hint: 240.21(B)(1)(4): the feeder device may not exceed 10 times the tap conductor ampacity.

steps.note: 240.21(B)(1)(4): field-installed taps up to 10 ft.

types.title: Garage receptacles (210.52(G)(1))
types.prompt: How many receptacle outlets are required in an attached garage with {bays} vehicle bays?
types.hint: 210.52(G)(1): at least one receptacle outlet for each car space (bay).

steps.text: One receptacle outlet per vehicle bay
steps.note: 210.52(G)(1), in addition to any for specific equipment.

types.title: Apprentices per licensee (Nebraska)
types.prompt: How many apprentice electricians may work with {lic} licensed journeymen?
types.hint: Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-2113(2): up to three apprentices per licensee.

steps.text: Up to {per} apprentices for each licensee
steps.note: Nebraska State Electrical Act, Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-2113(2).

types.title: Maximum overload setting (430.32(C))
types.prompt: A motor with a full-load current of {fla} A and {marking} will not start with the normal overload setting. What is the maximum overload trip rating permitted?
types.hint: 430.32(C) lets you go higher when the motor won't start: 140% for a service factor of 1.15 or more or a 40°C rise, 130% for all other motors.

vars.expr: pick(mk == 1, 'a service factor of 1.15', pick(mk == 2, 'a marked temperature rise of 40°C', 'a service factor of 1.0'))

show: pick(mk == 1, 'service factor 1.15 or more', pick(mk == 2, 'temperature rise 40°C or less', 'all other motors'))
steps.note: The normal settings in 430.32(A)(1) are 125% / 115%; 430.32(C) is the most you may go up to if the motor will not start.

types.title: Feeder for two motors (430.24)
types.prompt: A feeder supplies a {hp1} hp and a {hp2} hp, {V} V, {phase_name} motor. What minimum ampacity must the feeder conductors have?
types.hint: 430.24: 125% of the largest motor's full-load current plus 100% of the other motor's full-load current (table values).

steps.note: 430.24, using the table full-load currents (430.6(A)(1)).

types.title: Motor load in VA (three-phase)
types.prompt: What is the load in volt-amperes of a {hp} hp, {V} V, three-phase induction motor?
types.hint: Find the Table 430.250 full-load current, then VA = amps × volts × 1.732.

steps.note: Three-phase volt-amperes use √3 (1.732).
The question asks for the closest value.

types.title: Box fill with two wire sizes
types.prompt: What is the minimum volume required for a box containing {n1} {awg1:awg} conductors and {n2} {awg2:awg} conductors?
types.hint: Each size gets its own Table 314.16(B)(1) volume: count × volume for each size, then add.

steps.text: Volume = Σ (count × volume for that size)
steps.note: 314.16(B)(1): each conductor counts at the volume for its own size.

types.title: Total conductor area (Chapter 9, Table 5)
types.prompt: What is the total area of {n1} {awg1:awg} and {n2} {awg2:awg} {ins_name} conductors?
types.hint: Look up one wire's area for each size in Chapter 9, Table 5, multiply by the count, then add.

steps.text: Total = Σ (count × area of one wire)
steps.note: Areas from Chapter 9, Table 5 (THHN/THWN from its own section).

types.title: Space left in a raceway
types.prompt: How much space remains without exceeding the allowed fill when {n} {awg:awg} {ins_name} conductors are placed in trade size {ts} {rw_name}?
types.hint: 40% area of the raceway (Chapter 9, Table 4) minus the wires' total area (count × Table 5 area).

steps.note: Chapter 9, Table 1: over 2 wires may fill 40%.

types.title: Dwelling general lighting load (220.41)
types.prompt: What is the general lighting load for a dwelling with {area} ft² of floor area?
types.hint: 220.41: 3 VA per square foot, using the outside dimensions (220.5(C)). Open porches, garages and unused spaces are not counted.

steps.note: 220.41: 3 VA per ft², area from the outside dimensions (220.5(C)).

types.title: Small-appliance and laundry load (220.52)
types.prompt: A dwelling has {sa} small-appliance branch circuits and {lau} laundry circuit(s). What load is included for them in the service calculation?
types.hint: 220.52: 1,500 VA for each 2-wire small-appliance circuit and each laundry circuit.

steps.note: 220.52(A) and (B). At least two small-appliance circuits are required (210.11(C)(1)).

types.title: Number of lighting circuits
types.prompt: A dwelling has {area} ft². How many {amps} A, 120 V circuits are required for the general lighting load?
types.hint: Lighting VA = area × 3. One circuit carries 120 V × its amps. Divide, then round up to a whole circuit.

steps.note: 220.41 load; any fraction needs another circuit.

types.title: Fastened-in-place appliances (220.53)
types.prompt: {intro} What is their demand load on the service (standard method)?
types.hint: 220.53: four or more fastened-in-place appliances (not ranges, dryers, heat or A/C) may be taken at 75%.

vars.expr: 'A building has ' + fmt(n) + ' fastened-in-place water heaters rated ' + fmt(kw) + ' kW each.'

steps.text: {n} appliances is four or more: {tot} × 75% = {dem} kW

types.title: Small conductor protection (240.4(D))
types.prompt: What is the maximum overcurrent protection for a {size:awg} {metal_name} {ins} conductor in an ambient temperature of {ambient}°F with {ccc} current-carrying conductors?
types.hint: Correct the ampacity first, then remember 240.4(D): 14 AWG copper 15 A, 12 AWG copper 20 A, 10 AWG copper 30 A (aluminum 12 AWG 15 A, 10 AWG 25 A).

steps.text: OCPD ≤ corrected ampacity, and ≤ the 240.4(D) limit
steps.note: 240.4(D) applies after correction and adjustment factors.

show: pick(cap <= std, 'The 240.4(D) limit is the smaller value', 'The next standard size above ' + fmt(amp) + ' A (240.4(B)) is ' + fmt(std) + ' A')
steps.note: 240.4(B) allows the next standard size above the ampacity, but never more than 240.4(D).

types.title: Equipment grounding conductor (Table 250.122)
types.prompt: What is the minimum size {metal_name} equipment grounding conductor for a circuit protected by a {rating} A overcurrent device?
types.hint: Find the first Table 250.122 row whose rating is at least the device rating.

steps.text: Size by the overcurrent device rating
steps.note: 250.122(A): use the rating of the device ahead of the circuit, not the load.

steps.text: Table 250.122: {rating} A falls in the {row} A row → {egc:awg} {metal_name}
steps.note: Use the first row whose rating is not exceeded by the device.

types.title: Fraction to decimal
types.prompt: What is the decimal equivalent of {num}/{den} in.?
types.hint: Divide the top number by the bottom number.

steps.note: A fraction is a division problem.

types.title: Maximum neutral current (120/240 V)
types.prompt: On a 120/240 V system, Line 1 to neutral carries {p1} W and Line 2 to neutral carries {p2} W. What is the most current the neutral can carry with only one line on?
types.hint: With one line off, the neutral carries all of the other line's current: I = P ÷ 120 V for the larger load.

steps.note: When only one line is on, the neutral carries that line's full current.
The question asks for the closest whole number.
